statements.text: Congress needs to make sure artificial intelligence works for people and not the other way around. Giant corporations are putting profits ahead of people, pushing reckless experiments that risk global catastrophe for our family’s health, our kids’ future, and our paychecks. Nobody voted for this.
I have passed laws and co-sponsored laws that make sure that we protect Colorado's consumers and workers, while creating a reasonable floor that all businesses have to abide by.
statements.venue: Candidate statement quoted on AI on the Ballot

statements.text:
Trump is attacking my efforts that created safeguards for AI because I stand in the way of Trump and Musk's plot to enrich themselves. 

Coloradans deserve technology that works for everyone, not just billionaires. https://t.co/zZKB2bqCnJ

I’ve delivered on my promise to protect Coloradans from the risks of AI, passing common-sense laws that Gabe Evans opposed. I understand that important decisions around your family’s healthcare, your hard-earned job, and your fundamental rights should be decided by people, not harmful algorithms or powerful corporations.

AI can, of course, deliver real benefits. I will work tirelessly and use my experience and insights to make sure artificial intelligence works for people, not the
other way around.

(4/4)
I will also work to fund cyber defense for hospitals, water, and the grid against AI-enabled attacks. I also support age checks and parental controls on AI chatbots for minors, to keep kids safe online.

(3/4) 
(1) requiring large AI firms to report critical safety incidents in a timely manner 
(2) requiring independent safety reviews before major model releases 
(3) implementing protections for whistleblowers 
(4) holding AI firms that lie to the government about safety practices or infringe on privacy rights accountable 
(5) requiring notice before AI-driven layoffs at large employers

(2/4)
Families deserve strong protections, real accountability, and a fair shot. That's why I support policies that ensure AI companies are not above the law. 

That includes:

I’ve been thinking about the risks of AI for years, which is why I passed the first comprehensive AI bill in the country back in 2024 in the Colorado State House. It got bipartisan support.

We also got bipartisan support for my bill allowing whistleblowers at AI companies to come forward with catastrophic risks.

Bigger action is long overdue. 🧵

Tens of thousands of incidents of increasingly-powerful AI agents going rogue.

These AI companies are racing without guardrails towards powerful models that could put our families at risk and lead us to an existential crisis. 

Congress must act. Now. 
https://t.co/vPsI3ke6OX
statements.quoted:
SCOOP: OpenAI, Anthropic and security researchers are investigating tens of thousands of incidents - not dozens - in which their frontier models took steps that outside evaluators would consider problematic, sources told Axios.

The sheer volume of incidents found in our reporting indicate that the problem is orders of magnitude more complex than what is currently publicly known and disclosed.

The findings also raise questions about what level of control anyone working on AI development can expect to have over their own technology, and whether these kinds of incidents are becoming synonymous with frontier deployment.

Read my latest for Axios here: https://t.co/42h9aR4sem

statements.quoted:
The story keeps getting crazier. To recap everything that has been reported so far: 

- The US intelligence community discovered that Jensen Huang, the CEO of the largest company in the world, was sleeping with Alice Huang, a Chinese spy and an executive at Megaspeed. (FT)
- Multiple independent investigations have concluded that Megaspeed is likely a Chinese cutout, which helps Chinese companies access AI chips or circumvent export controls. (NYT and Bloomberg) 
- The US intelligence community also concluded that Alice Huang’s goal was to convince Jensen to lobby the U.S. government to loosen export controls on advanced AI chips. (NYT)
- The intelligence community relayed this information to “a small group of top US government officials” earlier this year. (FT)
- Over the last year, Jensen Huang has repeatedly lobbied the U.S. government to loosen export controls on advanced chips. @BISgov has done so, not only by permitting the export of H200 chips to China, but also not enforcing export controls that would have required a license for exports of the most advanced Blackwell chips to Megaspeed and Southeast Asia.
- Although @CommerceGov leadership was presumably briefed on this information by the U.S. intelligence community, @BISgov has taken no actions to tighten controls on Megaspeed or Southeast Asia. 
- Megaspeed remains a preferred cloud partner of Nvidia, and continues to receive Nvidia Blackwell chips despite employing a Chinese spy who reportedly is romantically engaged with the CEO of Nvidia. 
- Tens of billions of dollars worth of AI chips have been exported to Southeast Asia this year alone, and Malaysia and Singapore are now two of the four largest importers of AI chips in the world. 

What is going on here??? We need answers. The question of who gets the most advanced AI chips in the world is literally the defining strategic question of our time. And not only does it seem like the MSS may be directly influencing the debate on export controls in the United States, but also @CommerceGov is refusing to listen to the warnings of the IC on this issue. What is a POSSIBLE good explanation for why Megaspeed is still receiving chips? Why is there not a license requirement for AI chip shipments to all of Southeast Asia? This is beyond strange at this point. 

The fallout from this story will be massive. Obviously, the motivations underpinning Nvidia’s policy views opposing export controls must now all be questioned. But also, how did @BISgov sit on this information and has still taken no actions? We need answers.
